content: Idiopathic occipital lobe epilepsy (IOLE) is a type of epilepsy that falls under the category of idiopathic focal epilepsy syndromes. It was first described by Gastaut in 1982. IOLE is further divided into two subtypes: early-onset childhood epilepsy with occipital spikes, also known as Panayiotopoulos type or Panayiotopoulos syndrome, and late-onset childhood epilepsy with occipital spikes, referred to as Gastaut type. Additionally, idiopathic photosensitive occipital epilepsy, a reflex epilepsy syndrome, is also considered a form of IOLE. IOLE is generally considered a benign epilepsy syndrome, characterized by specific electroencephalographic (EEG) findings, including occipital sharp and slow wave complexes. Compared to benign rolandic epilepsy, IOLE is less common, accounting for approximately 20% to 30% of benign childhood partial epilepsies. The Panayiotopoulos type is reported to represent 6% to 13% of childhood focal epilepsies. Children with Panayiotopoulos type typically present at an average age of five years, with a range of one to 14 years. These children experience prolonged nocturnal seizures, which often begin with prominent autonomic and behavioral symptoms such as vomiting, pallor, and irritability. The prognosis for Panayiotopoulos type is excellent, with most children achieving seizure remission within one to two years. The Gastaut type is a rarer form of pure occipital epilepsy, accounting for 2% to 7% of benign childhood focal seizures. Children with Gastaut type usually present at an average age of eight years, with a range of three to 16 years. These seizures are frequent, brief, and occur during the daytime. They are characterized by initial visual symptoms, such as visual hallucinations (phosphenes), ictal blindness, or visual illusions. In 50% to 60% of cases, seizures remit within two to five years of onset. Idiopathic photosensitive occipital lobe epilepsy is classified as a reflex epilepsy syndrome with an age-related onset. It typically begins between the ages of five and 17 years and is more common in girls. Seizures in this subtype are often triggered by photic stimuli, such as television or video games, and can be stopped by removing the photic stimulus. Despite advances in understanding partial epilepsy syndromes with genetic underpinnings, the exact cause of IOLE remains unknown. Most patients with IOLE experience a benign course, but 40% to 50% of those with the Gastaut type may continue to have visual seizures and occasional secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Additionally, some children with IOLE may exhibit atypical disease progression or persistent neuropsychological deficits. The primary treatment for IOLE involves the use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs). Patients with IOLE generally respond well to AEDs, and the prognosis is favorable. Carbamazepine is the most commonly used AED, while valproate is often preferred in cases where photosensitivity is present. However, it remains unclear whether there are significant differences in efficacy among the various AEDs used to treat IOLE. Given the absence of abnormalities on laboratory tests and neuroimaging in IOLE, surgery is not typically considered a standard treatment. However, for patients with medically refractory occipital epilepsy, surgical intervention is increasingly being explored and may provide benefits. The precise mechanisms underlying IOLE are not yet fully understood. Different AEDs exert their antiepileptic effects by targeting voltage-dependent sodium, calcium, and potassium channels, as well as GABA receptors, excitatory amino acid receptors, enzymes, and synaptic proteins. For instance, carbamazepine primarily works by blocking voltage-dependent sodium channels, reducing their availability for activation. Surgical treatment, which involves removing the abnormal epileptic zone, may also be effective in stopping seizures. Although there are numerous pharmacological and surgical options for managing IOLE, the optimal approach to treatment and improving long-term outcomes remains uncertain. A systematic review of the effectiveness and safety of these treatments is necessary to better inform clinical practice and optimize patient care.
